doc.title: Bill Crow interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, October 18, 1995

title: Living at Birdland and the Basie band's arrival
summary: He haunts Birdland, hears Parker and the house band, and in 1953 plays opposite Basie while with Terry Gibbs.

story.theme_name: Coming to New York: clubs, jams, and making it
story.community_name: Making it in New York: arrival, clubs and the scene

blocks.x: Is this about the time you mentioned you saw the Basie band come in to Birdland?

Oh that was earlier. You know I became a denizen of Birdland as soon as I got to town. That was the one place that was available to me. That’s why I rented that first room a block away on 8th Avenue. I’d go down there every night because I didn’t have much of anyplace else to go. And I think the admission was less than a dollar then. And you could go down and sit in the bleachers and you didn’t have to spend another nickel, and listen to Charlie Parker, you know? He was there with his own band for the first two or three weeks I was in town and then it was, and the house band was just as strong, it was all the guys that had worked with Bird — Hank Jones and Miles, I think Red Rodney was with Bird at that time but Miles was in the house band. J.J. Johnson was in the house band, Max Roach was in the house band. It was wonderful. And they — everybody would come by and play or come by and listen. I got to know what all the musicians looked like anyway. Lester Young would be in the house and Art Tatum came in and sat in one night, and that was the first place I saw Jo Jones live. So it was someplace in the early 50s there, that Birdland decided to remodel and redecorate. They added some acoustical tiles and stuff like that so that they could put Basie in there once in a while. This was a new idea to put a big band in a small club like that. I guess it had been done on the street before, but not while I was around. So Basie had been working with a small group, just for economic reasons, and I think this was right at the time that he put the new band together. His managers talked Birdland, well I guess his managers were connected with Birdland in some kind of way. It was a whole small-time mob relationship there. I believe Morris Levy was known as a wise guy and his brother, who later got knifed in Birdland, was just a little like a street punk that everybody knew was mob connected. But they put the Basie band in there. I think the deal was that since it was in town and they would guarantee them something like three or four appearances a year, that they didn’t have to pay them their road salary. You know they would get the band at a bargain rate that way. So here comes the band. I was working with Terry Gibbs’ quartet about that time, so that must have been ‘52 or early 53, because I went with Thornhill—no, no, I was with Thornhill in ‘53 and then I went with Terry. So it was ‘53. We had this two week booking opposite the Basie band. I think it was the first time that they’d had Count in there.
